title: Acute gallstone pancreatitis: reading the bloods and scoring severity

header.contentArea: Emergency general surgery (blood results and arterial gas)
guidelineVersions: Revised Atlanta classification (Banks et al., Gut 2013)

brief.role: Core surgical trainee on call for general surgery
brief.scenario: Mrs Brenda Ashworth, 62, weighs 70 kg. She has had severe epigastric pain radiating to her back for 12 hours, with vomiting. She has known gallstones. HR 110, BP 105/65, RR 22, SpO2 95% on air, temperature 37.8°C. The examiner will show you her results in stages.
brief.task: Interpret the results, assess the severity of her illness, and outline your management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Diagnose, find the cause, then predict severity from the numbers you are given.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Calling it mild on admission bloods. The Glasgow score is completed at 48 hours.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Typical pain with a lipase over three times normal: acute pancreatitis, probably gallstone."

grid.label: Reads the admission data
grid.fail: Calls it cholecystitis, or says a CT is needed to make the diagnosis.
grid.pass: Typical pain plus lipase over three times the upper limit: acute pancreatitis. Gallstones on ultrasound make a biliary cause likely.
grid.high: States two of three criteria (pain, enzymes, imaging) confirm it, so CT adds nothing now; notes the duct is not dilated.

grid.label: Predicts severity
grid.fail: Scores only the admission bloods and calls it mild, or cannot name the criteria.
grid.pass: Uses worst values in 48 hours: age, white cells, calcium, albumin and PaO2 score 5. Three or more, or CRP over 150, predicts severe.
grid.high: Names all eight Glasgow criteria with cut-offs, and says scores predict severity; they do not classify it.

grid.label: Classifies by organ failure
grid.fail: Calls her severe on the score alone, or misses the respiratory failure.
grid.pass: PaO2 7.6 kPa on air is respiratory organ failure. Lasting over 48 hours makes it severe; resolving sooner, moderately severe.
grid.high: Works out PaO2/FiO2 about 270 mmHg, below 300. Mild means no organ failure and no local or systemic complications.

grid.label: Fluid resuscitation
grid.fail: Runs 250–500 mL/h for hours, or gives large fixed volumes without reassessing.
grid.pass: Goal-directed, moderate: Hartmann's 10 mL/kg bolus if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h, reassessing pulse, BP and urine output.
grid.high: Cites WATERFALL: aggressive fluid caused more fluid overload with no better outcome. Watches oxygen need closely as the PaO2 falls.

grid.label: Supportive care
grid.fail: Keeps her nil by mouth for days, or starts prophylactic antibiotics.
grid.pass: Oxygen, analgesia, catheter and fluid balance; eats if she can; no prophylactic antibiotics; critical care referral for organ failure.
grid.high: Enteral nutrition within 72 hours in moderately severe or severe disease; parenteral only if enteral fails or is contraindicated.

grid.label: Imaging
grid.fail: Requests CT on admission to stage the pancreatitis.
grid.pass: No routine CT at presentation. Contrast CT from 72–96 hours if she is not improving, to look for necrosis or collections.
grid.high: Early CT underestimates necrosis. CT sooner only if the diagnosis is in doubt.

grid.label: Gallstone plan
grid.fail: Books ERCP for pancreatitis alone, or discharges without a plan for her gallbladder.
grid.pass: ERCP only for cholangitis. Not a mild attack: delay cholecystectomy until any collections resolve or beyond 6 weeks.
grid.high: Same-admission cholecystectomy for mild attacks cuts readmission (PONCHO); in moderately severe or severe disease with collections, delay until they resolve or beyond 6 weeks.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The ALT is up and she has gallstones, so this is cholecystitis. I'd get a CT to be sure.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Her Glasgow score on these bloods is 2. Is she mild?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Yes, under 3, so it's mild pancreatitis.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: At 48 hours her PaO2 is 7.6 kPa on air.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd put her on oxygen. She's still mild on the score.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hartmann's at 500 mL an hour for the first day.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Nil by mouth to rest the pancreas, and meropenem to prevent infected necrosis.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: ERCP today to clear the duct.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Typical pain with a lipase over three times the upper limit: acute pancreatitis. Gallstones on ultrasound make it biliary.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Here are her results at 48 hours.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Using the worst values: age, white cells, calcium, albumin and PaO2 make a Glasgow score of 5. With a CRP over 150, severe disease is predicted.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A PaO2 of 7.6 on air is respiratory failure. If it lasts over 48 hours she has severe pancreatitis; if it resolves, moderately severe.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Goal-directed and moderate: a 10 mL/kg Hartmann's bolus as she's hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h, reassessing pulse, BP and urine output.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Oxygen, analgesia and a catheter. She can eat if she tolerates it. No prophylactic antibiotics. I'd refer her to critical care.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not routinely now. Contrast CT from 72 to 96 hours if she isn't improving.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: ERCP only if she develops cholangitis. With organ failure this isn't a mild attack, so I'd delay cholecystectomy until any collections resolve or beyond 6 weeks.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Two of three criteria are met, pain and lipase, so CT isn't needed for diagnosis. The duct is 6 mm, so no obstruction yet.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: PaO2 under 8 kPa, age over 55, white cells over 15, calcium under 2, urea over 16, LDH over 600, albumin under 32, glucose over 10. These predict severity; the Atlanta class depends on what actually happens.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How do you define organ failure?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: PaO2/FiO2 at or below 300 mmHg. Hers is about 270. Mild means no organ failure and no local or systemic complications.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: In WATERFALL, aggressive fluid caused more fluid overload without better outcomes. With her PaO2 falling, I'd watch her oxygen needs closely.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: If this becomes moderately severe or severe, I'd start enteral feeding within 72 hours; parenteral only if enteral fails.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Early CT underestimates necrosis. I'd scan sooner only if the diagnosis were in doubt.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Her bilirubin rises and she has rigors.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's cholangitis: blood cultures, antibiotics and ERCP within 24 hours. Same-admission cholecystectomy is for mild attacks, where it cuts readmission. In moderately severe or severe disease with collections, I'd delay it until they resolve or beyond 6 weeks.

failures.move: Scoring the admission bloods and calling her mild.
failures.consequence: Misses predicted severe disease; the score is only complete at 48 hours.
Fluid overload and worse respiratory failure, with no gain in outcome.

failures.move: Prophylactic antibiotics or prolonged nil by mouth.
failures.consequence: Against NICE advice; adds resistance and malnutrition risk without benefit.
Underestimates necrosis and adds contrast load without changing early management.
Procedural risk with no benefit when there is no cholangitis.

recovery.when: You lose count of the Glasgow score
recovery.line: PANCREAS: PaO2, Age, Neutrophils, Calcium, Renal (urea), Enzymes (LDH), Albumin, Sugar.
The score predicts it; persistent organ failure over 48 hours defines it.

knowledge.fact: Diagnosis needs two of: typical pain, lipase or amylase at least three times the upper limit, typical imaging.
Glasgow: PaO2 <8 kPa, age >55, WCC >15, calcium <2, urea >16, LDH >600, albumin <32, glucose >10 mmol/L. Worst values over 48 hours; 3 or more predicts severe.
CRP over 150 mg/L at 48 hours predicts severe disease.
Organ failure: modified Marshall score 2 or more (PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 mmHg). Persistent over 48 hours: severe.
About 15–20% of adults with severe acute pancreatitis die in hospital.
Contrast CT from 72–96 hours after onset, not routinely at presentation.

recall.think: Organ failure, especially respiratory, and cholangitis.
recall.say: "Glasgow 5 and CRP over 150: predicted severe. She has respiratory failure."
do: Oxygen, moderate goal-directed fluids, critical care referral

numbers.meaning: organ failure lasting this long means severe

recall.trap: A low score on admission bloods does not mean mild.
recall.finish: Same-admission cholecystectomy only if mild; with collections, delay until they resolve or beyond 6 weeks.

sources.name: Banks PA, Bollen TL, Dervenis C, et al. Classification of acute pancreatitis 2012: revision of the Atlanta classification and definitions by international consensus. Gut 2013;62:102–11
sources.supports: Diagnosis (two of three criteria, enzymes at least three times the upper limit); organ failure by modified Marshall score (PaO2/FiO2 ≤300); mild, moderately severe and severe definitions

sources.name: Working Party of the British Society of Gastroenterology et al. UK guidelines for the management of acute pancreatitis. Gut 2005;54 Suppl 3:iii1–9
sources.supports: Glasgow score 3 or more and CRP over 150 mg/L at 48 hours as predictors of a severe attack

sources.name: Blamey SL, Imrie CW, O'Neill J, et al. Prognostic factors in acute pancreatitis. Gut 1984;25:1340–6
sources.supports: Eight-factor (modified Glasgow) score measured within 48 hours of admission; three or more factors predicts severe disease

sources.name: de-Madaria E, Buxbaum JL, Maisonneuve P, et al. Aggressive or moderate fluid resuscitation in acute pancreatitis (WATERFALL). N Engl J Med 2022;387:989–1000
sources.supports: Moderate goal-directed regimen (10 mL/kg bolus if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h); aggressive fluid increased fluid overload (20.5% v 6.3%) without improving outcomes

sources.name: NICE NG104: Pancreatitis
sources.supports: No prophylactic antimicrobials (1.2.3); not nil by mouth without a clear reason (1.2.5); enteral nutrition within 72 hours in moderately severe or severe disease (1.2.6); parenteral only if enteral fails (1.2.7); 15–20% in-hospital mortality in severe disease (1.1.5)

sources.name: Working Group IAP/APA Acute Pancreatitis Guidelines. IAP/APA evidence-based guidelines for the management of acute pancreatitis. Pancreatology 2013;13(4 Suppl 2):e1–15
sources.supports: Initial contrast CT at least 72–96 hours after onset; early CT only for diagnostic doubt; no antibiotic prophylaxis; ERCP for cholangitis; same-admission cholecystectomy in mild biliary pancreatitis; in moderately severe or severe disease with peripancreatic collections, delay until collections resolve or beyond 6 weeks

sources.name: Tenner S, Vege SS, Sheth SG, et al. American College of Gastroenterology guidelines: management of acute pancreatitis. Am J Gastroenterol 2024;119:419–37
sources.supports: ERCP within 24 hours for cholangitis; cholecystectomy before discharge in mild biliary pancreatitis; CT reserved for diagnostic doubt or failure to improve

sources.name: da Costa DW, Bouwense SA, Schepers NJ, et al. Same-admission versus interval cholecystectomy for mild gallstone pancreatitis (PONCHO). Lancet 2015;386:1261–8
sources.supports: Same-admission cholecystectomy reduces readmission for recurrent gallstone-related complications

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Presentation of acute pancreatitis, Glasgow criteria and supportive management

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9 minutes with 1 minute's reading; examiner-led questioning in applied knowledge stations

media.task: Read the admission and 48-hour results and score severity
media.description: Results sheet laid out as a lab printout: admission bloods, ultrasound report and arterial gas, then the 48-hour set, with reference ranges

partner.opening: These are Mrs Ashworth's admission results. Talk me through them.

reveals.finding: Admission (12 hours from onset): lipase 2,450 U/L (ref <60). WCC 16.4, glucose 8.1, urea 7.2, adjusted calcium 2.21, albumin 36, LDH 410, bilirubin 34, ALT 220, ALP 190, CRP 38.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for imaging or the gas
reveals.finding: Ultrasound: multiple gallbladder stones, common bile duct 6 mm, no duct stones seen. Arterial gas on air: PaO2 10.4 kPa.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for repeat results or the 48-hour set
reveals.finding: 48 hours: WCC 15.2, glucose 9.2, urea 8.4, adjusted calcium 1.91, albumin 29, LDH 520, CRP 232. Gas on air: PaO2 7.6 kPa. HR 104, BP 112/70, urine output 0.6 mL/kg/h.

push.question: What is her Glasgow score, and what does it mean?
push.expect: 5 on worst values (age, WCC, calcium, albumin, PaO2); 3 or more predicts severe.

push.question: Is she severe?
push.expect: Respiratory organ failure now; severe if it lasts over 48 hours, otherwise moderately severe.

push.question: How much fluid would you give?
push.expect: Moderate, goal-directed: 10 mL/kg bolus if hypovolaemic, then 1.5 mL/kg/h; reassess.

push.question: When would you scan her?
push.expect: Not routinely now; contrast CT from 72–96 hours if not improving.

push.question: What about her gallbladder?
push.expect: Not a mild attack: delay cholecystectomy until any collections resolve or beyond 6 weeks; same-admission surgery applies to mild attacks. ERCP only for cholangitis.

curveballs.prompt: Her bilirubin rises to 90 and she has rigors.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Cholangitis: cultures, antibiotics, ERCP within 24 hours.

curveballs.prompt: At 96 hours she still needs 40% oxygen for a PaO2 of 9 kPa.
curveballs.safeAnswer: PaO2/FiO2 about 170 mmHg: persistent organ failure, so severe. Critical care and specialist centre advice.

curveballs.prompt: The nurse asks whether to keep her nil by mouth.
curveballs.safeAnswer: No, unless she is vomiting. Enteral nutrition within 72 hours if moderately severe or severe.
No prophylactic antibiotics. Treat proven infection only.
